lessons.application: Let the first mandatory shot teach a reliable rule: show or audibly localize nearby infected turning toward its sound. It is a lesson, not a punishment for an unavoidable tutorial action. Later encounters must let the player act on that lesson through firing position, timing or movement. Pitch an authored escape whose mistakes follow you, not simulation breadth the build does not contain.
lessons.successTest: Without coaching, a new player links the approaching zombies to the shot and deliberately changes their next engagement. Ask what they expect the full game to contain; broad sandbox expectations reveal a positioning mismatch.
lessons.doNotInfer: Historical concurrency is neither reachable marketing audience nor sales. Noise is an established mechanic; this sequence does not make it novel. Do not present off-screen scripted arrivals as proof of a city-wide simulation.

lessons.role: Why preparation belongs before the final horde
lessons.sourceFacts: The official game promise joins first-person survival and combat to crafting and tower-defense-style base protection. Its construction, traps, vehicles and destruction belong to a much broader established product.

kpis.label: Historical peak
kpis.evidence: Previously verified manual SteamDB observation, retained in the existing September 3 analysis

lessons.application: Give the required barricade a visible combat benefit, then let the final encounter test it. Reuse existing navigation and damage with one readable brute variation. The baseline has one barricade socket; alternate placements and richer building choices are later experiments. A boss climax makes the demo closer to action-survival defense than Zomboid's everyday simulation, so communicate that tone honestly.
lessons.successTest: Compare the configured encounter with and without the barricade internally. In the public test, players should identify the benefit of what they built and use it at least once. If the defense makes no difference, the crafting beat is ceremony. Two player-selected configurations are not required in this version.
lessons.doNotInfer: A mature game's audience does not validate a three-week production budget. The peak is historical, not September demand. This transfer does not require voxel destruction, free-form architecture or the competitor's full system catalogue.

lessons.role: Equipment handling that produces a decision; audience-matched distribution later
lessons.sourceFacts: The official game emphasizes preparation and manual equipment handling during a hazardous expedition. Separately, CM Games' authored Lock & Load account reports a themed multi-developer VR sale and Steam homepage exposure; that is distribution evidence, not a test of inventory design.

kpis.label: Lock & Load homepage exposure
kpis.window: Retrospective publication date; exact historical sale dates absent

applyTo: Grab inventory after the first shot
lessons.application: For this baseline, make equipment continuity legible: take the gun and bag, understand the bandage and construction materials, carry them through the vehicle transition and use them at camp. Let the player see each resource's purpose, with a safe first inventory lesson. An ammo-versus-repair packing trade-off is a later experiment, not a committed requirement that can make this demo unwinnable. Recruit survival/preparation-focused creators before broad variety outreach.
lessons.successTest: Ask what each carried item is for, then observe whether it survives the handoff and provides the expected use. Separate interface confusion from deliberate planning. This baseline does not claim to validate a full inventory-choice economy.
lessons.doNotInfer: VR handling demand does not automatically transfer to mouse and keyboard. The sale involved established participants, discounts and featuring; spend and incremental sales are unknown. No inventory mechanism is proven to have generated those impressions.

lessons.role: A familiar action plus a frightening consequence; footage followed by playable proof
lessons.sourceFacts: DREADMOOR combines familiar fishing and boat preparation with an unsettling survival setting. Its publisher describes a months-long mix of playtests, showcases, creator coverage, social activity and paid traffic. Official July news reported a later wishlist milestone.
lessons.application: Use the home as the recognizable place and the gunshot as the understandable action that changes its safety. Let the drive and brief camp preparation provide contrast before the final threat; constant combat leaves no safety to lose. Capture one continuous, truthful clip from immediate danger through the sound consequence, then a longer run proving the camp payoff. Treat creator access and an understandable build as prerequisites, not as last-day tasks.
lessons.successTest: Cold viewers can describe what the player did, why the next threat arrived and what they want to try. Demo players recognize the same interaction rather than discovering that the clip was only a staged vignette.
lessons.doNotInfer: The two milestones are not sales, a three-week result or isolated organic acquisition. Total spend is unknown and campaign windows overlap. The account's February IGN appearance and claimed March first contact leave a chronology ambiguity; do not reproduce that sequence as a precise acquisition recipe.

lessons.role: Existing controls are not the same as a convincing first-time experience
lessons.sourceFacts: The developer reported a six-minute median for a demo described as eight to ten minutes in its February 2024 Next Fest postmortem. On March 10, 2026, he documented camera stabilization and faster early movement after noticing the opening worked against the intended flow.

kpis.label: Median demo playtime
kpis.window: February 2024 Next Fest postmortem; day not asserted here

lessons.application: Test the actual packaged camera, aim response, hit feedback and door interaction before decorating the city. The first shot must feel like the advertised game. Avoid using slow walking, repeated empty looting or two equivalent herds to manufacture length. In the driving slice, camera, collisions, exit point and return-to-foot controls matter more than another street of props.
lessons.successTest: Mark the first confusing input, camera disturbance and unproductive wait in each cold run. Compare their locations, not merely total session duration. Test the encoded promotional video on a phone as well as the live build on the declared target PC.
lessons.doNotInfer: Six minutes is not a survival-demo target or a completion rate. The source has conflicting visit totals and a 420→755 wishlist endpoint difference of 335 versus a claimed 355; no conversion rate should be derived. A later feel patch does not establish its commercial effect.

lessons.role: Trailer craft: show the rule, then its complication
lessons.sourceFacts: Derek Lieu's August 8, 2026 retrospective explains showing basic herding before extra mechanics and allowing imperfect attempts to reveal challenge. He reports more than 100,000 IGN views for the resulting trailer; the trailer belonged to the November 2025 launch, not a new 2026 release.

kpis.label: Reported IGN trailer views
kpis.window: As reported in the retrospective; not launch-day views

lessons.application: The playable opening may begin with voices and suspense; the trailer need not reproduce its waiting. Begin footage close to the breach, preserve enough of the shot-and-response action to understand it, then demonstrate a different survival decision. Show a recoverable mistake and response. Save inventory grids, weapons, scenery and boss montage until the viewer understands why those features matter.
lessons.successTest: Show a short cut without explanatory narration to five target viewers. Ask them to describe the rule and one available response. Then test an audio-on version: sound is essential to this hook, so silent comprehension alone cannot validate the experience.
lessons.doNotInfer: This is a practitioner's editing account, not a randomized conversion study. IGN views are not wishlists, sales or an attainable baseline. The URL contains August 4, but the displayed publication date is August 8.

lessons.role: Choose whose pacing and agency the sequence serves
lessons.sourceFacts: Shiny Shoe's June 11, 2024 postmortem reports approximately 60% solo runs and 40% co-op, alongside different needs from those audiences. The statistic describes runs, not unique players or survival-genre preferences.

kpis.label: Reported solo/co-op run split
kpis.window: Historical post-launch observations; sample size and exact collection window undisclosed

lessons.application: For a solo slice, make every beat completable without a partner: inventory rules, driving and building cannot secretly assume another person watches the door. If co-op is already intended and supported, test pairs separately; who hears the cue, who triggers the breach, who owns the car and what an incapacitated player does all change the sequence. Do not add networking merely to make trailer incidents look social.
lessons.successTest: Keep solo and group observations separate. In the chosen mode, no player loses agency through an unexplained scene transition, forced inventory interaction or vehicle handoff. Ask whether the ending resolves the experience they were promised.
lessons.doNotInfer: Inkbound's run split cannot estimate the solo share of zombie survival demand. Its business-model and localization lessons are not evidence that this specific combat sequence will convert.

crucialLessons: If players enjoy shooting but cannot explain a preparation consequence, the slice currently proves a linear zombie action game, not survival crafting.
If the second herd and boss only increase enemy durability, the sequence escalates duration rather than decisions.
If resource gathering is enjoyable only because the player anticipates a much broader sandbox, disclose the intended scope and retest.
If trailer viewers cannot identify a controllable action, the footage may advertise atmosphere while leaving the actual game unclear.
If the first-time completion problem is a camera, interface, collision or softlock issue, fix the test before interpreting abandonment as weak genre demand.

pipelineFlow.output: Terrain shape, elevation and masks for city pad, exit road and rural camp.
pipelineFlow.gate: Known distances/grades match the player and vehicle; preserve source plus export settings.

pipelineFlow.output: A coherent city kit with tested collision, scale, navigation and LOD/material policy.
pipelineFlow.gate: Home, two encounter spaces and garage work before background district density expands.

pipelineFlow.output: Reusable room/door/furniture generator outputs, baked to native assets for the demo.
pipelineFlow.gate: Generate and package one playable house before three variants; preserve editable source separately.

pipelineFlow.output: First-person body/hands if supported, base infected variants and a brute using compatible rigs.
pipelineFlow.gate: Weapon alignment, retargeting, hit reactions and measured crowd cost pass in the real scene.

pipelineFlow.output: Each critical model mapped to the existing inventory item's ID, icon, stack and use/recipe behavior.
pipelineFlow.gate: A model being game-ready does not by itself prove pickup, UI or save behavior.

pipelineFlow.output: Complete sequence with checkpoints, vehicle, camp, horde/boss and end screen.
pipelineFlow.gate: Measured run on the named target PC, including cold start, retries and the heaviest encounter.

artDirection.mood: Grounded outbreak tension with brief relief after reaching the rural camp. Home feels inhabited, streets disrupted and camp modest but visibly player-made.
artDirection.consistency: Choose one architectural period, weather/time-of-day treatment and material palette across asset packs. Use a fixed lighting setup for the slice rather than building a day/night simulation.
artDirection.readability: Warm familiar home light, a distinct exit landmark and a readable camp silhouette. Contrast identifies paths and enemies; avoid relying only on color to communicate danger.
artDirection.characters: MetaHuman detail is most valuable at close range; choose actual gameplay assemblies and cheaper enemy variants based on profiling. Face detail is secondary to attack silhouette, rig compatibility and hit feedback.
artDirection.interiors: Treat Houdini as a repeatable authoring aid. Leave room for manual placement of the first gun, breach, pickups and sightlines; procedural variation must not scramble critical teaching moments.

performance.target: On day one, name the target PC, resolution and graphics preset. If the chosen target is 60 FPS, its frame-time reference is 1000/60 ≈16.7 ms; that is a proposed product target, not a vendor or asset-pack guarantee.
performance.measure: Record CPU/GPU frame time, memory/VRAM, loading hitches and active-AI count during the heaviest street/finale and maximum-speed drive. Use packaged cold-start and repeat runs; distinguish profiler overhead from ordinary play.
performance.priority: Keep input response, enemy tells, collision and objective continuity before high-fidelity hair, decorative density or resolution. Existing engine features must be measured in this project; a rendering feature does not remove AI or animation cost.
performance.qualityGate: Choose numerical frame-time and memory acceptance targets after the representative day-one measurement. Until hardware and trace results exist, do not label the demo optimized or promise a crowd capacity.
